Under all those circumstances we are not at all surprised that the Danes should have rejected Lord I'almerston's terms of mediation. For the Germans to withdraw from a territory they had invaded, and for the Danes to withdraw from a territory secured by treaty and inheritance to their Sovereign, was not an equilateral 'concession Hut the question was not one of right alone or of diplomatic arbitration : the plain English of the matter is, that the Danes are by no means disposed to submit to such an injustice as the German invasion of Sehleswig, and that the Gourt of Copenhagen now feels that, in spite of the losses this struggle has occasioned, the lot of Denmark is far less unenviable than that of its powerful enemies. In Denmark there is a loyal and united people, a gallant navy, a bold army, and a Government strong in the affections of the people and in some of the greatest alliance of Europe ; in Germany the nation is torn and distracted by a blind and feverish paroxysm, even the mi litar v forces of lh5 Confederation are not equal to what they were supposed to he, the Government has nowhere the real confidence of the people or the authority of the state, and as for alliances it is still uncertain to which side Germany may look for support. NEW MODE OF CULTIVATING THE SUGAR CANE. prom a correspondent In describing tiie detail of cultivation which it would be advisable to pursue, I would suggest that canes should be planted not closer than at a square of len feet ; this arrangement would permit the spread of the stools, sions, corn, or what not, between the rows o and allow of a cultivation of provicane roots, from the bottom to the summit of the hills. Corresponding to these petty farms, in suitable situations and at reason able distances one from another, there should be established small sugar factories, at which the pioprietor or lessee might also keep a liquor shop and store, (a suit of mullum in parvo) at which all the warns of the surrounding population might be metþÿ and thus a complete system of reciprocity between the manulactor and the labouring farmer he originated. To facilitate (Ins object, and to give an impetus to industry, the Government should lend out money on interest, (reasonable security lor the repayment being given) to build and slock these establishments and set them goingþÿ and premiums should be offered to encourage the forma lion ol such. 1 would, by no means, advise ihe establishment of small distilleries connecied with these factories. On the contrary it would be better entirely to disjoin the department of sugar making from the distillery. On or two distilleries would he sufficient for a parish, and on such an onlarged scale might be conducted to greater

advantage than on a limned principle. Fac tories, according to the paitern 1 suggest, being placed on favorable siles, would be come, in process of time, iht: nucleus of vil lages. The carriage of molasses and provi sions thence to the distilleries would raise up a department of carriers. The improve mem of roads would necessarily follow, tus tie and business would be the concomimnt and an example of industry being dmlv presented to view, would necessarily mlecl others, hitherto unemployed, and impel them to < xeition. Almost every hill in St. Andrew, and 1 might add throughout the island, is suited to the growth of stiff cane if treated in the way 1 suggest, and immense quantities of sugar might be made from tracts of land which now either lies idle, or merely subserves by the growth ol provisions and corn to home consumption. The system suggested also has the advantage of offering inducements to intelligent immigrants, and would afford active employmerit to persons resident in the island who are unable to engage in manual field labor, and yet might become very useful members of society in tlie capacity of carriers, or laboring sugar factors, tailoring distillers, and the like The master (actors and their (am ilies, according to the plan laid down, would at once form a class ol middlemen, so much needed in this islandþÿ nor would it even be necessary for the factor to (mild his own factory, because the tiiiliiv of Ihe principle being acknowledged, the outlay might, and

would, no doubt, be made bv the capitalist as a profitable investment, and rented out to the factor, as is the ease with corn mills in other countries. The system I suggest is not the offspring of lo dayþÿ it has been the slow growth of Joyg experience and þÿ o b s e r v a t i o n and a. the

time slavery received ns death blow in this island 1 foresaw and predicted dial the estivation ot large plantations hett.tr i sugar or coffee) must decline, and siumer oi later give place lo a new and more li.mied Iona of cultivation. Sound arises from vibrations of the air, as may be seen by the vibiattons in the water of a musical glass, and by the affections of light bodies laid on strings in concord ; and they may beJell by the vibrations of all instruments. The delicacy and intensity with which they reach the car, proves the extreme fullness of space in aerial atoms. We distinguish tones when the vibrations are 7000 in a second, and therefore the particles must be less than the 5G000th of art inch asunder. considering the gravest tone as the eighth of an inch. This coincides, loo, with waves of light, which appear, in red, tube the 40,000th of an inch asunder, and in violet the 04,000th. The lowest tone which the ear can discriminate is, according to some, 12| undula-

tions in a second, and, to others, 30 : and, the most acute, above 0000. Every sourd is a mixture of 3 tones, just ns a ray of light is of 3 colours. The union of the key-note with the 5th and 10th, is the common chord. The diatonic scale is the prism of sound. Sounds are distinct at twice the distance on water that they arc on land. The velocity of waves of sound, in an elnslic medium, is equal to the velocity of a body falling through the half atmosphere or heights of the modulus of elasticity, or half 27,8(10 feet. The fire of the English, on landing in Egypt, was distinctly heard 130 miles. Dr. Jamieson s«\s, in calm weather he heard every word of a sermon at the distance ol 2 miles. Sounds are more intense as the air is denser. In the Arctic regions, petsons can converse at more than a mile distant, when the thermometer is below zero." The report of a distant gun is heard before the word fire, which directs the discharge. Water is a better conductor of sound than air. Wood, also, is a powerful conductor of sound, arid so is flannel or ribbon.
